doc.title: Scott Robinson interviewed by Monk Rowe,Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997

title: Playing tenor at the festival; Lester Young and Slam Stewart
summary: Robinson discusses rarely playing tenor and his love of Lester Young, including singing a Young record solo with Slam Stewart.

story.theme_name: Lester Young: the man, the sound, the Basie years
story.community_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound

blocks.x: Very good competition. It’s a little daunting sometimes when you get some guys up there playing a whole lot of tenor. I go through long periods of not playing any tenor because I get calls to play a lot of baritone and bass clarinet and whatever. So now suddenly I get to play the tenor which I love. But on the other hand it takes me a little while to get over feeling like an idiot. By the end of the set I didn’t feel like an idiot, but at the beginning of the set I really did feel like an idiot. But that’s all part of the fun.
I hear some Lester Young in what you play. Am I off the mark with that?

No certainly not. Lester is I think my favorite clarinet player and a great composer and great tenor player. My first ‘78 I ever bought was Lester Young, “Sometimes I’m Happy” and “Afternoon of a Basie-ite” on Keynote with Johnny Guarnieri and Slam Stewart. And I was just telling Phil Atterbury from the Mississippi Rag that I met Slam Stewart in a club in Annapolis, Maryland and I went up and I said, “You know I’ve have this great record that you’re on and it meant so much to me through the years.” And he says, “Oh, yeah, “Sometimes I’m Happy — do you remember my solo on that?” And he started singing it. And I knew it very well because I’d listened to the record a hundred times. So we were standing in the club singing this solo together. It was a great moment. Everybody is like what are those two doing? But I was amazed that he would just — that was, what was that, 1943 or some time. I don’t remember the year. But I was amazed that he could just remember his solo off of that record and just say “oh yeah, I remember that” and start singing it. It’s amazing. I still can’t get over that.
